questions.q: Antiretroviral drugs can lower HIV in the blood to very low levels, yet the infection cannot be cured. The main reason is that:
o: Viral DNA integrated in long-lived host cells stays hidden and inactive
HIV is a bacterium resistant to all drugs
The drugs destroy all helper T cells
HIV can live freely outside cells for years
questions.x: As a provirus, HIV DNA sits silently inside the chromosomes of resting cells, where drugs and the immune system cannot reach it. When treatment stops, these cells can start making virus again.

questions.q: A few weeks after infection with HIV, many people develop:
o: No change at all at any stage
A short flu-like illness with fever, sore throat and rash
questions.x: The acute stage of HIV infection, 2–4 weeks after exposure, often causes a brief flu-like illness. Opportunistic infections appear years later, when helper T cells have fallen very low.

questions.q: Gram for gram, protein respired as a fuel releases an amount of energy that is:
o: Almost zero, because proteins are never respired
questions.x: Protein and carbohydrate each give roughly 17 kJ (4 kcal) per gram, about half of what fat gives. Protein is respired, especially in starvation.

questions.q: In the Krebs cycle, FADH2 is formed at the step in which:
questions.x: The enzyme succinate dehydrogenase removes hydrogen from succinate, forming fumarate, and FAD accepts it to become FADH2. The malate step reduces NAD+, not FAD.

questions.q: When glucose changes from its straight-chain form to its ring form, the aldehyde group on carbon 1 reacts with the –OH group on:
questions.x: The C-1 aldehyde reacts with the C-5 hydroxyl group, so the ring contains carbons 1 to 5 and one oxygen. Carbon 6 stays outside the ring.

questions.q: The order of codons in an mRNA corresponds directly to the:
o: Order of genes on the chromosome
Order of amino acids in the polypeptide
Number of ribosomes in the cell
Order of tRNA molecules in the cytoplasm
questions.x: Codons are read one after another, and each adds its amino acid in turn, so the codon order fixes the amino acid order.

questions.q: On complete hydrolysis, a lipid yields only a long-chain alcohol (not glycerol) and a long-chain fatty acid. The lipid is:
questions.x: A wax is an ester of a long-chain fatty acid with a long-chain alcohol other than glycerol. Triglycerides and phospholipids give glycerol, and a glycolipid would also give a sugar.

questions.q: A tripeptide is completely hydrolysed. How many water molecules are used, and how many product molecules are formed?
questions.x: A tripeptide has three amino acids joined by two peptide bonds. Breaking each bond uses one water molecule, so 2 water molecules give 3 free amino acids.

questions.q: A protein that is permanently combined with a non-protein part is called a:
questions.x: A conjugated protein consists of a protein plus a non-protein (prosthetic) group, as in glycoproteins, lipoproteins and nucleoproteins. A simple protein contains amino acids only.

questions.q: The enzyme that breaks triglycerides into fatty acids and glycerol during digestion is:
questions.x: Lipase hydrolyses the ester bonds of triglycerides, releasing fatty acids and glycerol. Amylase and maltase digest carbohydrates, and pepsin digests proteins.

questions.q: The movement of sodium (Na⁺) and potassium (K⁺) ions across cell membranes is essential for:
questions.x: Nerve impulses depend on Na⁺ and K⁺ moving across the neurone membrane. Chlorophyll needs magnesium and thyroxine needs iodine.

questions.q: Beadle and Tatum found that each mutant strain of Neurospora could grow only if one particular nutrient was supplied. This showed that each mutation:
o: Destroyed the mould's ability to make one specific enzyme
Changed every enzyme of the mould
Affected only the mould's cell wall
questions.x: Each mutant lacked one enzyme of a pathway, so it could not make one nutrient and needed it supplied. This led to the idea that one gene controls one enzyme.

questions.q: Which of the following sugars is a pentose?
questions.x: Deoxyribose has five carbon atoms. Galactose and fructose are hexoses (six carbons), and glyceraldehyde is a triose (three carbons).

questions.q: The layer of fat around organs such as the kidneys and heart is useful because it:
o: Speeds up enzyme reactions in the organs
Protects the organs from mechanical shock
questions.x: Fat cushions delicate organs and protects them from knocks, besides storing energy. It does not carry oxygen, store genes or act as an enzyme.

questions.q: Which mRNA codon has no matching tRNA and causes the ribosome to stop?
questions.x: UAG is one of the three stop codons (with UAA and UGA). AUG codes for methionine, UGG for tryptophan and GUA for valine.

questions.q: Sucrose is obtained commercially from:
questions.x: Table sugar (sucrose) is extracted from sugarcane and sugar beet. Milk gives lactose, barley malt gives maltose, and cotton and wood are mainly cellulose.

questions.q: Which of the following eukaryotic cells has no cell wall?
questions.x: Plants and most algae have cellulose walls and fungi have chitin walls, but animal cells are bounded only by the plasma membrane.

questions.q: According to the endosymbiont hypothesis, chloroplasts arose from:
o: Photosynthetic prokaryotes, like cyanobacteria, taken into an early eukaryotic cell
Vesicles budded off the Golgi apparatus
questions.x: Chloroplasts are thought to descend from cyanobacteria-like cells engulfed by an ancestral eukaryote; their own DNA, 70S ribosomes and double membranes support this.

questions.q: The red, purple and blue colours of many petals are due to water-soluble anthocyanin pigments stored in the:
questions.x: Anthocyanins are dissolved in the cell sap of the vacuole. Chromoplasts hold fat-soluble carotenoids, which give yellow and orange colours.

questions.q: Which stage of aerobic respiration does NOT take place inside the mitochondrion?
o: Oxidation of pyruvate to acetyl CoA
questions.x: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm. Pyruvate then enters the mitochondrion, where its oxidation, the Krebs cycle and electron transport take place.

questions.q: An impulse travelling along an axon does not spread back over the part it has just passed because:
o: Myelin always blocks ions behind the impulse
That part of the membrane is still in its refractory period
Behind the impulse the membrane stays permanently depolarised
The Na+ concentration behind the impulse falls to zero
questions.x: The membrane just behind the action potential is refractory, so local currents can only trigger the resting membrane ahead. This keeps conduction one-way along the axon.

questions.q: Damage to the brain is often permanent because mature neurons:
o: Normally do not divide to replace lost cells
questions.x: Mature neurons do not undergo cell division, so lost neurons are not replaced. They do have a nucleus and make proteins actively.

questions.q: A weak stimulus depolarises a small patch of axon membrane but does not reach threshold. The result is:
o: A small action potential that travels more slowly
A small local change that fades away without an impulse
A full action potential that travels only halfway
A burst of several small impulses
questions.x: Below threshold there is only a small local depolarisation that dies away. Action potentials are all-or-none and do not come in small sizes.

questions.q: How many ventricles are there in the human brain?
questions.x: There are two lateral ventricles (one in each cerebral hemisphere), a third ventricle in the diencephalon and a fourth ventricle in the hindbrain, four in all.

questions.q: The olfactory bulbs, which receive impulses from the smell receptors of the nose, are part of the:
questions.x: The olfactory bulbs project forward from the underside of the cerebrum and belong to the forebrain. The midbrain and hindbrain lie behind and below.

questions.q: The pituitary gland hangs below the brain, attached by a stalk to the:
questions.x: The pituitary is joined by a short stalk to the hypothalamus at the base of the forebrain. This close link lets the hypothalamus control the pituitary.

questions.q: The dura mater is the:
o: Innermost meninx attached to the brain surface
Tough, outermost meninx lying next to the skull
questions.x: The dura mater is the thick, tough outer layer of the meninges. The arachnoid is the web-like middle layer and the pia mater is the thin inner layer on the brain surface.

questions.q: The cytoplasm inside an axon is called the:
questions.x: The cytoplasm of an axon is axoplasm. Sarcoplasm is muscle-fibre cytoplasm and nucleoplasm is inside the nucleus.

questions.q: Two enzymes have activity curves that peak at pH 2 and pH 8 respectively. These enzymes are most likely:
questions.x: Pepsin of the acidic stomach works best near pH 2, while trypsin of the small intestine works best in slightly alkaline conditions near pH 8.

questions.q: At any one moment, a single active site normally holds:
o: Only one substrate molecule (or one set of reacting molecules)
questions.x: Each active site binds one substrate (or one set of reactants) at a time, converts it and releases the products before binding again.

questions.q: The substrate concentration is 100 times that of a competitive inhibitor with similar binding strength. The inhibition will be:
questions.x: Competitive inhibition depends on the relative amounts of substrate and inhibitor. With a large excess of substrate, most active sites hold substrate.

questions.q: Sucrase hydrolyses one molecule of sucrose into:
questions.x: Sucrose is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose. Two glucose units come from maltose, and glucose plus galactose from lactose.

questions.q: In the small intestine, inactive trypsinogen is converted into active trypsin by:
questions.x: Enterokinase (enteropeptidase) from the intestinal lining activates trypsinogen. Hydrochloric acid activates pepsinogen in the stomach, not trypsinogen.

questions.q: The two scientists who proposed the chemical-evolution hypothesis in the 1920s were Oparin and Haldane. Their nationalities were, respectively:
questions.x: A.I. Oparin was a Russian (Soviet) biochemist and J.B.S. Haldane was a British scientist; they reached similar ideas independently.

questions.q: Which explanation of the great speed of the cheetah is Lamarckian?
o: Ancestors ran hard to catch prey, their leg muscles grew stronger and this was inherited
Faster cheetahs caught more prey, survived and passed on their speed
Speed arose because slow cheetahs were eaten by lions
Speed came from a mutation that spread by chance
questions.x: Lamarck's explanation relies on effort during life (use) followed by inheritance of the gain. Survival of individuals that were already faster is the Darwinian explanation.

questions.q: The process by which individuals with favourable variations survive and reproduce more than others was named by Darwin:
questions.x: Darwin called it natural selection. Artificial selection is done by humans, and use and disuse is Lamarck's idea.

questions.q: The white scar-like tissue left in the ovary after the corpus luteum degenerates is the:
questions.x: When the corpus luteum breaks down it is replaced by fibrous tissue called the corpus albicans ('white body').

questions.q: Menopause, the end of menstrual cycles at about 45 to 55 years of age, occurs because:
o: The pituitary stops making FSH and LH
The ovaries stop responding to FSH and LH, so oestrogen and progesterone fall
The uterus is removed by the body
questions.x: At menopause the ovaries run out of responsive follicles, so oestrogen and progesterone fall. With less negative feedback, FSH and LH actually rise.

questions.q: After about the first three months of pregnancy, most of the progesterone is produced by the:
questions.x: The corpus luteum maintains progesterone early in pregnancy; later the placenta takes over this role and the corpus luteum declines.

questions.q: The main purpose of the monthly changes in the uterus is to:
o: Prepare the endometrium to receive an embryo
questions.x: Each cycle the endometrium is built up so that a fertilised egg could implant. If no pregnancy occurs, it is shed and the cycle starts again.

questions.q: Which structure is NOT found in a skeletal muscle fibre?
questions.x: Intercalated discs join neighbouring cardiac muscle cells and are absent from skeletal muscle. Skeletal fibres do have sarcoplasmic reticulum, T-tubules and Z lines.

questions.q: As a myosin head swings and pulls actin in the power stroke, which molecules leave it?
questions.x: ADP and phosphate are released as the head swivels in the power stroke. A new ATP then binds to detach the head; calcium stays with troponin, and acetylcholine acts only at the sarcolemma.

questions.q: The joint between the lower jaw (mandible) and the skull, which moves during chewing and speaking, is a:
questions.x: The jaw joint moves freely and has a fluid-filled cavity, so it is a synovial joint. The other skull bones are joined by immovable fibrous sutures.

questions.q: The large opening in the base of the skull through which the spinal cord passes is the:
questions.x: The spinal cord leaves the cranium through the foramen magnum in the occipital bone. The obturator foramen is an opening in the hip bone.

questions.q: The main role of osteocytes in mature bone is to:
questions.x: Osteocytes are mature bone cells trapped in lacunae; they maintain the living bone matrix. Dissolving bone is the job of osteoclasts, and blood cells are made by red marrow.

questions.q: Which is the most abundant type of cartilage in the human body?
questions.x: Hyaline cartilage is the commonest type: it covers joint surfaces, forms the costal cartilages and supports the nose, trachea and bronchi. Elastic cartilage and fibrocartilage occur in far fewer places.

questions.q: Septic (infective) arthritis is caused by:
o: Infection of a joint by microorganisms such as bacteria
The immune system attacking the joint lining
questions.x: Septic arthritis is inflammation of a joint due to infection, usually by bacteria. Urate crystals cause gout, autoimmunity causes rheumatoid arthritis, and wear causes osteoarthritis.

questions.q: The stored carbohydrate broken down in skeletal muscle to provide glucose for making ATP during exercise is:
questions.x: Muscle stores carbohydrate as glycogen, which is broken down to glucose for respiration. Starch and cellulose are plant polysaccharides, and sucrose is a plant sugar.

questions.q: A colour-blind father and a carrier mother have daughters. These daughters are expected to be:
o: Half carriers and half homozygous normal
questions.x: Every daughter gets the father's Xᶜ. From the mother she gets Xᶜ or a normal X with equal chance, so half are colour-blind and half are carriers.

questions.q: Crossing over in a coupling dihybrid (AB/ab) always produces Ab and aB gametes in about equal numbers because:
o: Ab gametes are always more viable than aB
Crossing over occurs between sister chromatids
Each crossover is a reciprocal exchange between two chromatids
questions.x: In a crossover two non-sister chromatids swap segments, so each event gives one Ab and one aB chromatid.

questions.q: When the father is colour-blind and the mother heterozygous, the expected fraction of colour-blind children, sons and daughters together, is:
questions.x: XᶜY × XᶜX gives XᶜXᶜ, XᶜX, XᶜY and XY in equal numbers. Two of the four (a daughter and a son) are colour-blind, which is 1/2.

questions.q: A normal human sperm contains how many chromosomes in all?
questions.x: A sperm is haploid: 22 autosomes plus one sex chromosome (X or Y), 23 in total.

questions.q: In birds, which use the ZW system, a male bird has the sex chromosomes:
questions.x: In birds the male is homogametic (ZZ) and the female heterogametic (ZW), the reverse of humans.

questions.q: If Xᶜ stands for the colour-blindness allele, a colour-blind man has the genotype:
questions.x: A man has one X and one Y; the gene is on the X only. So a colour-blind man is XᶜY. The Y carries no allele for this gene.

questions.q: A woman with hemophilia (XʰXʰ) marries a normal man. Their children are expected to be:
o: Half the sons hemophilic and all daughters normal non-carriers
All sons normal and all daughters hemophilic
All sons hemophilic and all daughters carriers
questions.x: Every child gets an Xʰ from the mother. Sons have no other X and are hemophilic; daughters also get the father's Xᴴ and are carriers.

questions.q: The allele for red–green colour blindness is called recessive because:
o: It is found only in males
It is carried on the Y chromosome
It appears in every generation of a family
A carrier woman with one copy has normal colour vision
questions.x: A heterozygous woman sees colours normally: the normal allele masks the colour-blindness allele. That is what makes it recessive.

questions.q: Just after it leaves the heart, the pulmonary trunk divides into the:
questions.x: The pulmonary trunk splits into a right and a left pulmonary artery, one to each lung. Pulmonary veins bring blood back, and coronary arteries branch from the aorta.

questions.q: A student counts the pulse at her wrist as 72 per minute. Her heart rate is:
o: Impossible to tell from the pulse
questions.x: Each pulse wave is produced by one ventricular contraction, so the pulse rate equals the heart rate.

questions.q: The average mass of a healthy adult human heart is about:
questions.x: An adult heart weighs roughly 250 to 350 g, so about 300 g. 30 g is far too light, and 1.5 kg is closer to the mass of the liver.

questions.q: A network of capillaries supplying a tissue is called a:
questions.x: Capillaries form a branching network, the capillary bed, in every tissue. A portal system is two capillary beds joined by a vein.

questions.q: Coating of a bacterium with antibodies, so that phagocytes engulf it more readily, is called:
questions.x: In opsonisation antibodies act as markers on the pathogen's surface that phagocytes recognise. Agglutination is clumping, neutralisation is blocking a toxin, and precipitation is forming insoluble complexes.

questions.q: IgM is a pentamer made of five basic antibody units. How many antigen-binding sites does one IgM molecule have?
questions.x: Each basic Y-shaped unit has two binding sites. Five units joined together give 5 × 2 = 10 antigen-binding sites.

questions.q: Lymphocytes, the main cells of the specific immune response, are a kind of:
questions.x: Lymphocytes are white blood cells (agranulocytes) found in blood, lymph and lymphoid organs.

questions.q: Alveolar macrophages (dust cells) found in the alveoli function to:
o: Secrete mucus to keep the alveoli moist
Carry oxygen from the alveoli to the capillaries
Contract to push air out of the alveoli
Engulf dust particles and microbes that reach the alveoli
questions.x: Macrophages wander over the alveolar surface and engulf particles and bacteria that escape the mucus and cilia higher up. Oxygen crosses by diffusion, and alveoli have no contractile cells.

questions.q: A person breathes 12 times a minute with a tidal volume of 500 mL. If the dead space is 150 mL, how much fresh air reaches the alveoli each minute?
questions.x: Only 500 − 150 = 350 mL of each breath reaches the alveoli. 350 mL × 12 = 4200 mL per minute. 6000 mL is the total air breathed, and 1800 mL is the volume that only fills the dead space.

questions.q: The inspiratory reserve volume is the:
o: Air left in the lungs after a forceful expiration
Air breathed in during one quiet breath
Extra air that can be breathed in by force after a normal inspiration
Extra air that can be forced out after a normal expiration
questions.x: Inspiratory reserve volume is the additional air taken in by a deepest possible breath beyond a normal inspiration (about 3000 mL). The extra air forced out after a normal expiration is the expiratory reserve volume.

questions.q: Humans cannot digest the cellulose in plant food because they:
o: Do not produce the enzyme cellulase
Have a stomach too weak to grind it
Absorb cellulose whole without digesting it
questions.x: No human digestive gland secretes cellulase, so cellulose passes through undigested as dietary fibre (roughage). This fibre adds bulk to the faeces and helps peristalsis.

questions.q: At the junction of the ileum with the large intestine there is a valve. Its main role is to:
o: Release bile into the large intestine
Stop air from entering the colon
Control the passing of faeces from the rectum
Stop the contents of the caecum flowing back into the ileum
questions.x: The ileocaecal valve lets material pass from the ileum into the caecum but prevents backflow. Faeces are controlled by the anal sphincters, and bile enters at the duodenum.

questions.q: On a cold day a person puts on a woollen jacket and drinks hot tea. These are examples of:
questions.x: These are actions the person chooses, i.e. behavioural thermoregulation, alongside the automatic physiological responses.

questions.q: The term for animals, such as most bony fishes, whose chief excretory product is ammonia is:
questions.x: Ammonotelic animals excrete ammonia, ureotelic animals urea and uricotelic animals uric acid.

questions.q: Removing undigested food as faeces is called egestion, not excretion, because:
o: Faeces leave through the anus, not the urethra
Most of the faeces was never part of the metabolism of body cells
Excretion refers only to the removal of water
questions.x: Excretion removes waste products of the body's own metabolism, such as urea and carbon dioxide. Undigested food never entered the cells, so passing it out is egestion.

questions.q: Tubular secretion takes place mainly in the:
questions.x: Tubule cells of the PCT and DCT, close to the peritubular capillaries, move substances such as H+ and K+ from the blood into the tubule. The glomerulus filters but does not secrete.

questions.q: Water reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct is called 'facultative' because it:
o: Always occurs at a fixed rate
Varies with the body's needs, under the control of ADH
Takes place by active pumping of water
questions.x: The amount of water taken back in these parts depends on how much ADH is present, so it changes with hydration. This adjustable step is the basis of osmoregulation.

questions.q: Which set of blood results fits untreated kidney failure?
o: Raised urea, raised potassium, more acidic blood
Low urea, low potassium, more alkaline blood
Raised urea, low potassium, more alkaline blood
Low urea, raised potassium, normal pH
questions.x: Failing kidneys cannot excrete urea, potassium or hydrogen ions, so all three build up: urea and potassium rise and the blood becomes more acidic.

questions.q: The urge to urinate arises when:
o: The kidneys stop filtering the blood
Stretch receptors in the bladder wall are stimulated as it fills
The blood urea level rises above normal
questions.x: As urine collects, the bladder wall stretches. Stretch receptors send impulses to the spinal cord and brain, producing the urge to urinate.

questions.q: Some cancer treatments kill very large numbers of cells at once. This can cause uric acid stones because:
o: Dead cells release oxalate into the blood
The drugs raise blood calcium directly
Nucleic acids from the dead cells are broken down, releasing purines that form uric acid
questions.x: In humans purines from nucleic acids are broken down to uric acid. Massive cell death floods the blood and urine with uric acid, which can crystallise.

questions.q: Besides keeping water and salt in balance, the kidneys help control blood pressure mainly by:
o: Pumping blood back towards the heart
Adjusting blood volume through the amount of water and salt retained
questions.x: Keeping back more salt and water raises blood volume and pressure; excreting more lowers them. This links the kidney's osmoregulatory work to blood pressure.

questions.q: In the ELISA test, used for example to detect HIV infection, an antibody is linked to an enzyme so that:
o: A colour change shows that the target has been bound
The virus in the sample is destroyed
The antibody can enter the patient's cells
questions.x: When the enzyme-linked antibody is bound in the test well, adding the enzyme's substrate produces a coloured product. The colour indicates the presence of the antigen or antibody being tested for.

questions.q: Which set of temperatures matches the three steps of a PCR cycle (denaturation, primer annealing, extension) in that order?
questions.x: DNA strands separate at about 95 °C, primers bind at about 50–60 °C and Taq polymerase extends them at about 72 °C, its optimum. The cycle then repeats.

questions.q: An 'edible vaccine' is produced by:
o: Mixing killed bacteria into ordinary food
Drying a live vaccine and adding it to sugar
Inserting a gene for a pathogen's antigen into a food plant so its tissues make the antigen
questions.x: In edible vaccines a transgenic plant, such as potato or banana, expresses an antigen of a pathogen. Eating the plant tissue could then stimulate immunity without injection.

questions.q: A DNA probe test for Mycobacterium tuberculosis in sputum is valuable mainly because:
o: It kills the bacteria in the sample
It works without any bacterial DNA being present
It gives a result quickly, whereas culturing these slow-growing bacteria takes weeks
It is a vaccine as well as a test
questions.x: Tuberculosis bacteria grow very slowly, so culture can take several weeks. A probe detects their DNA directly, allowing much quicker diagnosis and treatment.

questions.q: For 2Ca + O₂ → 2CaO, 8 g of calcium is heated in 1.6 g of oxygen and 4.48 g of CaO is collected. What is the percentage yield? (Ca = 40, O = 16)
questions.x: Ca = 0.2 mol needs 0.1 mol O₂, but O₂ = 1.6/32 = 0.05 mol, so O₂ is limiting: CaO = 0.1 mol = 5.6 g. Yield = 4.48/5.6 × 100 = 80%. Treating calcium as limiting gives 11.2 g and a wrong 40%.

questions.q: 2.4 g of magnesium ribbon is dropped into a solution containing 0.1 mol of HCl: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. What volume of hydrogen forms at STP? (Mg = 24)
questions.x: Mg = 0.1 mol would need 0.2 mol HCl, so HCl is limiting. 0.1 mol HCl gives 0.05 mol H₂ = 1.12 dm³. 2.24 dm³ wrongly treats magnesium as limiting.

questions.q: Compared with a photon of violet light, a photon of red light has:
o: More energy and a longer wavelength
Less energy and a longer wavelength
Less energy and a shorter wavelength
More energy and a shorter wavelength
questions.x: Red light has a longer wavelength and lower frequency than violet light, so each red photon carries less energy (E = hc/λ).

questions.q: A photon of which kind of electromagnetic wave carries the least energy?
questions.x: Radio waves have the lowest frequency (longest wavelength) of these, and photon energy E = hν is smallest for the lowest frequency.

questions.q: When the electron of a hydrogen atom is promoted to an outer orbit, its total energy:
o: Stays the same in every orbit
questions.x: Eₙ = −1312/n² kJ mol⁻¹, so a larger n gives a smaller negative value, i.e. a higher energy. It stays negative while the electron is bound.

questions.q: A gas that would obey PV = nRT exactly at every temperature and pressure is called:
questions.x: An ideal gas obeys the gas laws exactly under all conditions. Real gases, including the noble gases, only approach this at low pressure and high temperature.

questions.q: At STP, which sample has the largest volume? (H 1, He 4, O 16, Cl 35.5)
questions.x: 4 g of H₂ is 2 mol, which occupies 44.8 dm³. Each of the other samples is 1 mol, which occupies 22.4 dm³.

questions.q: Charles's law applies when the amount of gas and which other quantity are kept constant?
questions.x: Charles's law relates volume and temperature for a fixed amount of gas at constant pressure. Density changes as the volume changes.

questions.q: Compared with the molecules of a gas, the molecules of a liquid are:
o: Much closer together, with little empty space between them
Much farther apart, with more empty space
Arranged in a fixed regular lattice
The same distance apart, but moving faster
questions.x: Liquid molecules are packed closely with little free space. A gas is mostly empty space, and a regular lattice belongs to a crystalline solid.

questions.q: The normal boiling point of a liquid is its boiling point at an external pressure of:
questions.x: Normal boiling point is measured at standard atmospheric pressure, 1 atm = 760 mm Hg. For water it is 100 °C.

questions.q: Which crystal system has a ≠ b ≠ c, with two angles equal to 90° and the third not equal to 90°?
questions.x: Monoclinic (as in monoclinic sulphur) has α = γ = 90° and β ≠ 90°. Orthorhombic has all angles 90°.

questions.q: Crystals of potassium chloride are hard and are not easily scratched. This is because:
o: Covalent bonds join each potassium atom to a chlorine atom
Hydrogen bonds hold the potassium and chloride ions together
Strong electrostatic attractions act between oppositely charged ions in all directions
Free electrons move through the lattice and bind the ions
questions.x: In an ionic crystal each ion is held by strong, non-directional electrostatic attractions to all its oppositely charged neighbours, so the lattice resists scratching. KCl has no covalent bonds, hydrogen bonds or free electrons.

questions.q: In the law of mass action, the active mass of a substance in solution is taken as its:
questions.x: Active mass means molar concentration, written in square brackets, e.g. [H₂]. The rate is proportional to the product of active masses.

questions.q: Suppression of a salt's solubility by adding an ion it already contains is explained by:
questions.x: Adding an ion already present in an equilibrium shifts it to use up that ion, as Le Chatelier's principle predicts.

questions.q: For a first-order reaction, a graph of rate (y-axis) against the concentration of the reactant (x-axis) is:
o: A curve that rises more and more steeply
A straight line with a negative slope
A straight line passing through the origin
questions.x: For rate = k[X], rate is directly proportional to [X], giving a straight line through the origin with slope k. A horizontal line belongs to a zero-order reaction.

questions.q: In three runs at one temperature: tripling [X] alone makes a reaction 9 times faster; then doubling [Y] as well makes it 18 times faster than the first run. What is the overall order?
questions.x: Tripling [X] gives 9 times the rate, so order 2 in X (3² = 9). Doubling [Y] then doubles the rate (9 to 18), so order 1 in Y. Overall 2 + 1 = 3.

questions.q: For a zero-order reaction, the units of the rate constant k are the same as the units of:
questions.x: For zero order, rate = k[X]⁰ = k, so k has the units of rate, mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

questions.q: Ethene burns: C₂H₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O(l). Using enthalpies of formation C₂H₄ +52, CO₂ −394 and H₂O(l) −286 kJ mol⁻¹, find its molar heat of combustion.
questions.x: ΔH = [2(−394) + 2(−286)] − (+52) = −1360 − 52 = −1412 kJ mol⁻¹. Adding the +52 instead of subtracting it gives −1308.

questions.q: The enthalpy of solution of a substance is the enthalpy change when one mole of it:
o: Dissolves in exactly 1 dm³ of water
Dissolves in so much solvent that further dilution causes no heat change
Is formed from its ions in solution
questions.x: Enthalpy of solution is measured at infinite dilution, when adding more solvent gives no further heat change.

questions.q: Of the four reactions shown, which one involves a transfer of electrons between atoms?
questions.x: Zinc falls from +2 to 0 and carbon rises from 0 to +2. In the other reactions no element changes its oxidation number.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of chlorine in potassium chlorate, KClO₃?
questions.x: +1 + x + 3(−2) = 0, so x = +5. The value +7 belongs to chlorine in perchlorate, KClO₄.

questions.q: In the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, the nitrogen atom is:
questions.x: Nitrogen has four σ bond pairs and no lone pair in NH₄⁺, so it uses four sp³ hybrid orbitals arranged tetrahedrally.

questions.q: The bond in a hydrogen molecule, H₂, is formed by:
o: Overlap of two 1s orbitals, giving a pi bond
Overlap of two 1s orbitals, giving a sigma bond
Overlap of a 1s and a 2p orbital
questions.x: Each hydrogen atom has only a 1s orbital. Two s orbitals can only overlap head-on, so the bond is a σ (s–s) bond.

questions.q: A molecule AB₂ is bent with a bond angle of about 104.5°. How many lone pairs are on the central atom A?
questions.x: Four electron pairs (two bonding, two lone) give the bent shape with an angle near 104.5°, as in water. With no lone pair AB₂ would be linear.

questions.q: A few drops of phenolphthalein are added to water after sodium has reacted with it. The solution turns pink because it contains:
questions.x: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂; the NaOH formed makes the solution alkaline, turning phenolphthalein pink.

questions.q: The first four ionisation energies of element X are 738, 1451, 7733 and 10540 kJ mol⁻¹. X is most likely in:
questions.x: The big jump comes after the second electron, so X has two outer electrons and the third comes from an inner shell; X is a Group II element (magnesium).

questions.q: Which gaseous ion has exactly four electrons in its 3d subshell?
questions.x: Mn is 3d⁵ 4s²; removing the two 4s electrons and one 3d electron gives Mn³⁺ = 3d⁴. Fe³⁺ and Mn²⁺ are 3d⁵, and Cr³⁺ is 3d³.

questions.q: Aliphatic compounds are best described as:
o: Compounds that contain a benzene ring
Ring compounds that contain an atom other than carbon
Open-chain compounds, with straight or branched chains
Compounds made only of carbon atoms
questions.x: Aliphatic means open-chain (acyclic). Alicyclic compounds are rings that resemble them in properties; benzene-ring compounds are aromatic.

questions.q: Applying the same idea used for benzene, the carbonate ion, CO₃²⁻, has three equivalent contributing structures, each with one C=O and two C–O bonds. The bond order of each C–O bond in the hybrid is about:
questions.x: Four bonding pairs (one double and two single bonds) are shared equally over three C–O bonds: 4/3 ≈ 1.33. Benzene's bond order of 1.5 comes from two structures, not three.

questions.q: A few drops of cold, dilute alkaline KMnO₄ are added to a gas jar of ethene and shaken. What is seen?
o: The purple colour disappears and a brown precipitate forms
A white precipitate forms and the solution stays purple
The solution turns from orange to green
questions.x: Ethene reduces MnO₄⁻, so the purple colour fades and brown MnO₂ appears, while ethene is oxidised to the diol. Orange to green is the change for dichromate.

questions.q: In the nitrating mixture, the role of concentrated sulphuric acid is to:
o: Act as the electrophile that attacks benzene
Supply sulphur that enters the ring
Reduce nitric acid to nitrogen dioxide
Protonate nitric acid so that it forms the nitronium ion, NO₂⁺
questions.x: H₂SO₄ is the stronger acid; it protonates HNO₃, which then loses water to give NO₂⁺: HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻.

questions.q: The C=C bond length in ethene is about:
questions.x: The C=C bond in ethene is about 1.34 Å, shorter than the C–C bond in ethane (1.54 Å) and longer than the C≡C bond in ethyne (1.20 Å).

questions.q: Phenol, C₆H₅OH, undergoes electrophilic substitution much faster than benzene because the –OH group:
o: Donates electron density to the ring
Withdraws electron density from the ring
Removes the π electrons from the ring
Makes the ring carbons sp³ hybridised
questions.x: The lone pair on oxygen is delocalised into the ring, raising its electron density and making it more attractive to electrophiles.

questions.q: When a vicinal dihalide is converted into an alkyne by dehydrohalogenation, the number of molecules of hydrogen halide removed from each molecule is:
questions.x: Each elimination removes one HX and forms one π bond. Two eliminations convert the single C–C bond into a triple bond.

questions.q: When ethylbenzene, C₆H₅CH₂CH₃, adds three moles of H₂ over Ni, the compound formed is:
questions.x: Hydrogen adds to the ring (3 mol H₂ per mole) while the ethyl side chain is already saturated, giving ethylcyclohexane, C₆H₁₁CH₂CH₃.

questions.q: 2-Bromobutane is heated with alcoholic KOH. According to Saytzeff's rule, the main product is:
questions.x: Saytzeff's rule says the more substituted alkene is the main product, so H is lost from C-3 to give CH₃CH=CHCH₃. But-1-ene forms too but in smaller amount; butan-2-ol would need aqueous KOH.

questions.q: In the SN1 mechanism, the slow, rate-determining step is:
o: Attack of the nucleophile on the carbocation
Simultaneous bond making and bond breaking
Removal of a proton from the β-carbon
Ionisation of the C–X bond to give a carbocation and X⁻
questions.x: SN1 has two steps: the slow heterolysis of C–X to form a carbocation, then fast attack by the nucleophile. Simultaneous bond making and breaking describes SN2.

questions.q: When bromine water converts one mole of phenol fully into its white tribromo product, the inorganic by-product formed is:
questions.x: C₆H₅OH + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃OH + 3HBr. Each substitution replaces one ring H by Br, and that H leaves with the other Br atom as HBr, so 3 mol HBr form.

questions.q: Propan-1-ol is warmed with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ and the product is distilled off as soon as it forms. The product is:
questions.x: A primary alcohol is first oxidised to an aldehyde; removing it at once stops further oxidation to propanoic acid. Propanone would come from the secondary alcohol, propan-2-ol.

questions.q: The carbon–oxygen double bond of a carbonyl group consists of:
o: One σ bond and two π bonds
One σ bond and one π bond
questions.x: Every double bond has one σ bond (head-on overlap of sp² and p orbitals) and one π bond (sideways overlap of unhybridised p orbitals).

questions.q: Methanal, HCHO, differs from all other aldehydes because its carbonyl carbon is bonded to:
o: One hydrogen atom and one alkyl group
One alkyl group and one –OH group
questions.x: In methanal both remaining bonds of the carbonyl carbon go to H atoms. Other aldehydes have one H and one alkyl or aryl group; ketones have two carbon groups.

questions.q: Acid-catalysed hydrolysis of an ester is reversible, but hydrolysis with aqueous NaOH goes to completion. The reason is that in alkaline hydrolysis:
o: NaOH is a stronger catalyst than H⁺
The acid formed is converted to its carboxylate ion, which does not react with the alcohol
The ester is converted into an amide
questions.x: The carboxylate anion cannot be attacked by the alcohol to re-form the ester, so the back reaction is removed and hydrolysis is complete.

questions.q: Fluoroethanoic acid, FCH₂COOH, is a stronger acid than chloroethanoic acid, ClCH₂COOH, because:
o: Fluorine releases electrons towards the carboxyl group
The C–F bond breaks more easily than the C–Cl bond
Fluorine is more electronegative and has a stronger electron-withdrawing inductive effect
questions.x: The stronger −I effect of fluorine pulls more electron density from the carboxylate ion, stabilising it and making H⁺ loss easier.

questions.q: Proteins that supply all the essential amino acids are called complete (first-class) proteins. Which food is a good source of such protein?
questions.x: Animal proteins such as those in eggs, milk and meat contain all the essential amino acids. Cereal proteins are short of some of them, such as lysine.

questions.q: Silicone sealant adhesives are widely used around bathroom fittings and in aquariums because, once set, they:
questions.x: Set silicone remains rubbery and is not attacked by water, so it seals wet joints that move slightly. A brittle or water-soluble adhesive would fail in these uses.

questions.q: The adjacent sides of a parallelogram are 5 cm and 4 cm long with an angle of 30° between them (sin 30° = 0.5). Using the vector product, the area of the parallelogram is:
questions.x: Area = |P × Q| = PQ sin θ = 5 × 4 × 0.5 = 10 cm². 20 cm² forgets the sin θ factor.

questions.q: A force on a 2 kg body at rest rises uniformly from zero to 20 N in 0.4 s. Using the area under the force–time graph, the speed of the body after 0.4 s is:
questions.x: Impulse = area of the triangle = ½ × 20 × 0.4 = 4 N s. This equals the change in momentum, so v = 4 ÷ 2 = 2 m s⁻¹. 4 m s⁻¹ forgets the ½.

questions.q: A 4 kg cart rolling at 5 m s⁻¹ couples with a stationary 6 kg cart, and they move off together. Their common speed is:
questions.x: Momentum before = 4 × 5 = 20 kg m s⁻¹. After: (4 + 6)v = 20, so v = 2 m s⁻¹. 3.3 m s⁻¹ wrongly divides by the 6 kg mass alone.

questions.q: A ball spends 2 s in the air before landing back at launch level. How high did it rise? (g = 10 m s⁻², no air drag)
questions.x: It rises for 1 s, so the initial vertical velocity is 10 m s⁻¹. H = (10)² ÷ (2 × 10) = 5 m, which equals gT²/8.

questions.q: The average velocity of a body over a time interval is zero. This tells us that:
o: Its final position is the same as its initial position
It was at rest throughout the interval
Its average speed was also zero
questions.x: Zero average velocity means zero displacement: the body ended where it began. It may still have moved and accelerated in between, so its average speed need not be zero.

questions.q: A shell at rest breaks into two pieces of 3 kg and 2 kg. The 3 kg piece moves off at 4 m s⁻¹. The velocity of the 2 kg piece is:
o: 6 m s⁻¹ in the same direction as the 3 kg piece
6 m s⁻¹ opposite to the 3 kg piece
4 m s⁻¹ opposite to the 3 kg piece
2.7 m s⁻¹ opposite to the 3 kg piece
questions.x: Total momentum stays zero: 3 × 4 = 2 × v, so v = 6 m s⁻¹, in the opposite direction.

questions.q: Ignoring air resistance, which statement about the velocity of a projectile launched at an angle is correct?
o: Its direction changes continuously during the flight
It is constant throughout the flight
Its direction stays the same but its magnitude changes
It is always directed vertically downward
questions.x: The velocity is along the tangent to the curved path, so its direction changes all the time. Its magnitude also changes as the vertical component changes.

questions.q: A body is raised through the same height on the Moon (g about one-sixth of Earth's) as on the Earth. The gravitational potential energy it gains on the Moon is:
o: Six times that on the Earth
The same as on the Earth
Zero, because the Moon has no air
One-sixth of that on the Earth
questions.x: PE = mgh and the mass and height are the same, so the PE is proportional to g: one-sixth of the Earth value. Air has nothing to do with it.

questions.q: The energy stored in food and fuels such as petrol and coal is:
questions.x: Food and fuels store energy in chemical bonds; it is released as heat and work when they react, for example during burning or respiration.

questions.q: Starting from rest, a grinding disc of radius 0.25 m speeds up at 4 rad s⁻². Three seconds later, what are its tangential acceleration and its rim speed?
questions.x: a = rα = 0.25 × 4 = 1 m s⁻². After 3 s, ω = αt = 12 rad s⁻¹, so v = rω = 0.25 × 12 = 3 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: A flywheel turns through an angular displacement of 4π rad. How many complete turns has it made?
questions.x: Each turn is 2π rad, so 4π rad corresponds to 4π/2π = 2 turns.

questions.q: An artery narrows to half its normal cross-sectional area. Blood (taken as an ideal fluid of density 1000 kg m⁻³) flows at 0.2 m s⁻¹ in the normal part. The fall in pressure in the narrowed part is:
questions.x: By continuity v₂ = 0.4 m s⁻¹. ΔP = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) = 500 × (0.16 − 0.04) = 60 Pa. Forgetting the ½ gives 120 Pa.

questions.q: When blood pressure is measured with a sphygmomanometer, the cuff is first pumped up above the systolic pressure so that:
o: Blood flows faster and more smoothly through the artery
The artery in the arm is squeezed shut and no blood flows through it
The diastolic pressure can be read immediately
The heart rate is slowed down
questions.x: Above systolic pressure the cuff closes the brachial artery completely. As the cuff is slowly released, blood begins to spurt through, giving the first sounds.

questions.q: Water (density 1000 kg m⁻³) flowing at 4 m s⁻¹ in a horizontal pipe is brought to rest at the front face of a small obstacle. Using Bernoulli's equation, the pressure there is greater than in the moving stream by:
questions.x: With v₂ = 0, ΔP = ½ρv₁² = 500 × 16 = 8000 Pa. Forgetting the ½ gives 16 000 Pa; forgetting to square gives 2000 Pa.

questions.q: A transverse wave travels along a stretched rope. At the instant a particle of the rope is at a crest, its velocity is:
questions.x: At a crest the particle is at its maximum displacement, where it stops for an instant before moving back. Particles move fastest as they pass through the mean position.

questions.q: Two tuning forks of frequencies 300 Hz and 302 Hz are sounded together. The time between two successive loud sounds (waxings) is:
questions.x: Beat frequency = 302 − 300 = 2 Hz, so a loud sound comes every 1/2 = 0.5 s.

questions.q: A particle performs SHM with angular frequency 4π rad s⁻¹. Its time period is:
questions.x: T = 2π/ω = 2π/4π = 0.5 s. Its frequency is 2 Hz.

questions.q: In its fundamental mode, a string held at both ends has how many nodes and antinodes, including the ends?
questions.x: The fundamental is a single loop: a node at each fixed end and one antinode in the middle.

questions.q: A wave in which the particles of the medium vibrate back and forth along the same line as the wave travels is called:
questions.x: In a longitudinal wave the particle vibrations are parallel to the direction of travel, producing compressions and rarefactions. In a transverse wave they are perpendicular to it.

questions.q: When SHM is represented as the projection of a point moving uniformly round a circle, the time period of the SHM equals:
o: The time for one complete revolution of the point
The time for half a revolution
The time for a quarter of a revolution
questions.x: In one revolution the projection moves from one end of the diameter to the other and back, completing one full oscillation.

questions.q: For an ideal gas the ratio γ = Cp/Cv is 1.4. Using Cp − Cv = R, its molar specific heat at constant volume Cv is:
questions.x: Cp = 1.4Cv, so 1.4Cv − Cv = R, giving 0.4Cv = R and Cv = R/0.4 = 2.5R. Then Cp = 3.5R, which is the tempting wrong choice.

questions.q: In the equation Q = nCΔT, where n is the number of moles, the quantity C is the:
o: Heat capacity of the whole body
questions.x: With amount measured in moles, the constant is the molar specific heat. In Q = mcΔT, with mass in kg, c is the specific heat.

questions.q: A 1 kg copper block (specific heat 420 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 100 °C is dropped into 0.1 kg of water (specific heat 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 20 °C. Ignoring losses, the final common temperature is:
questions.x: The heat capacities are equal: 1 × 420 = 0.1 × 4200 = 420 J K⁻¹. So the block falls and the water rises by equal amounts, meeting halfway at 60 °C.

questions.q: The potential difference between two points in an electric field is:
o: The force per unit charge between the two points
The work done per unit positive charge in moving a charge from one point to the other
The total charge flowing between the two points
The work done per unit time in moving charge between them
questions.x: Potential difference is work per unit charge (J C⁻¹). Force per unit charge is the electric field; work per unit time is power.

questions.q: The SI unit of the permittivity of free space, ε₀, is C² N⁻¹ m⁻². This is equivalent to:
questions.x: Since 1 F = 1 C V⁻¹ = 1 C² J⁻¹ = 1 C² N⁻¹ m⁻¹, C² N⁻¹ m⁻² equals F m⁻¹. N m² C⁻² is the unit of k, the reciprocal kind of quantity.

questions.q: Electric field strength, E = F/q₀, is classified as:
o: A vector quantity, with both magnitude and direction
A scalar quantity, with magnitude only
Always directed towards a positive charge
questions.x: E = F/q₀ is force per unit charge, and force is a vector, so E is a vector. The field points away from positive charges, not towards them.

questions.q: Wire P has length L and cross-sectional area A. Wire Q, of the same metal at the same temperature, has length 2L and area 2A. Compared with P, the resistance of Q is:
questions.x: R = ρL/A. Doubling L doubles R and doubling A halves it, so the two effects cancel and the resistance is unchanged.

questions.q: A battery is being charged, so current is driven through it opposite to its normal direction. Its terminal potential difference V is:
o: Greater than its emf, V = E + Ir
Less than its emf, V = E − Ir
Equal to its emf at all currents
questions.x: When charging, the charger must supply the emf plus the drop across the internal resistance, so V = E + Ir, larger than the emf.

questions.q: Only 0.05 Wb of flux passes through a 0.2 m² coil placed in a 0.5 T field. What angle does the field make with the coil's normal? (cos 60° = 0.5)
questions.x: Φ = BA cos θ gives cos θ = 0.05/(0.5 × 0.2) = 0.5, so θ = 60°.

questions.q: A transformer takes 500 W from the supply and delivers 450 W to its load. Its efficiency is:
questions.x: Efficiency = output/input × 100% = 450/500 × 100% = 90%. A real transformer cannot exceed 100%.

questions.q: For a coil of N turns in which the flux through each turn changes by ΔΦ in time Δt, Faraday's and Lenz's laws give the induced emf as:
questions.x: The emf equals the number of turns times the rate of change of flux, ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt; the minus sign shows Lenz's law.

questions.q: In the electromagnetic spectrum, microwaves lie between:
questions.x: In order of decreasing wavelength the spectrum runs radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.

questions.q: The large current through a forward-biased PN junction is carried mainly by:
o: Immobile ions in the depletion region
questions.x: Forward bias lowers the barrier so holes from the p-side and electrons from the n-side (majority carriers) cross in large numbers. Minority carriers give the tiny reverse current.

questions.q: Using 1/λ = R(1/1² − 1/2²) with R = 1.1 × 10⁷ m⁻¹, the wavelength of the first Lyman line of hydrogen is about:
questions.x: 1/λ = 1.1 × 10⁷ × 3/4, so λ = 4/(3.3 × 10⁷) ≈ 1.21 × 10⁻⁷ m = 121 nm. 91 nm is the Lyman series limit and 656 nm is the first Balmer line.

questions.q: Alpha particles from a radioactive source can be stopped completely by:
o: A few millimetres of aluminium only
questions.x: Alpha particles have a very short range and are stopped by paper or a few centimetres of air. Beta needs a few mm of aluminium; gamma needs thick lead or concrete to reduce it.

questions.q: Radiation damage that appears in the exposed person, such as skin burns, hair loss or cancer, is called a:
questions.x: Somatic effects show up in the person who was exposed. Genetic effects arise from damage to reproductive cells and appear in later generations.

questions.q: Which line contains both alliteration and a simile?
o: "The tired traveller trudged up the hill."
"The tired traveller trudged on like a turtle."
"Our guest walked as slowly as a tortoise."
"The path was a ribbon of silver."
questions.x: 'Tired traveller trudged ... turtle' repeats the 't' sound, and 'like a turtle' is a simile. The second line has only alliteration, the third only a simile, and the last is a metaphor.

questions.q: Report in indirect speech: Ayesha said, "I have finished my homework."
o: Ayesha said that she has finished my homework.
Ayesha said that she had finished her homework.
Ayesha said that I had finished her homework.
Ayesha said that she finished my homework.
questions.x: The present perfect 'have finished' becomes past perfect 'had finished', and 'I/my' become 'she/her'.

questions.q: Choose the word that best fits: "The starving child ___ his food so fast that he nearly choked."
questions.x: To 'gulp' is to swallow quickly in large amounts, which fits eating so fast he nearly choked; 'sipped' and 'nibbled' suggest small amounts.

questions.q: Which of these is a simple sentence?
o: The farmer was tired, so he walked home.
The tired old farmer walked slowly home after sunset.
The farmer walked home when the sun set.
Although he was tired, the farmer walked home.
questions.x: A simple sentence has only one clause; the first has one subject and one verb, however long it is.

questions.q: Choose the correct verb: "This time tomorrow, we ___ over the Arabian Sea on our way to Muscat."
questions.x: 'This time tomorrow' describes an action in progress at a future moment, which needs the future continuous.

questions.q: Change into the passive voice: "Ali had posted the letters before noon."
o: The letters were posted by Ali before noon.
The letters have been posted by Ali before noon.
The letters had been posted by Ali before noon.
The letters had posted by Ali before noon.
questions.x: The past perfect passive is 'had been' + past participle.

questions.q: In "She is extremely careful with her money", the adverb 'extremely' modifies:
questions.x: 'Extremely' is an adverb of degree telling how careful she is, so it modifies the adjective.

questions.q: Choose the correct word: "The lecture was so ____ that half the class fell asleep."
questions.x: An -ing adjective describes what causes the feeling: the lecture was 'boring'. The students would be 'bored', which describes how a person feels.

questions.q: Choose the correct word: "Pens, paper and envelopes are sold at the ____ shop."
questions.x: 'Stationery' (with -ery) means writing materials. 'Stationary' (with -ary) is an adjective meaning not moving.

questions.q: Ali, Bilal and Hamza scored different marks in a test. Ali did not score the highest. Hamza did not score the lowest. Bilal scored more than Hamza. Which statement must be true?
questions.x: Bilal beat Hamza, so Hamza is not highest; Hamza is not lowest either, so he is in the middle. Ali is not highest, so Ali is lowest and Bilal highest.

questions.q: Find the next number: 5, 9, 16, 29, 54, ?
questions.x: Each term is double the one before, minus 1, 2, 3, 4 in turn: 5x2-1=9, 9x2-2=16, 16x2-3=29, 29x2-4=54. So 54 x 2 - 5 = 103.

questions.q: Find the missing number: 7, 28, ?, 448, 1792
questions.x: Each term is 4 times the one before: 28 x 4 = 112, and 112 x 4 = 448 checks.

questions.q: Introducing a woman, Bilal said, "Her mother is the wife of my father's father." How is the woman related to Bilal?
questions.x: The wife of Bilal's father's father is Bilal's grandmother. Her daughter is his father's sister, that is, his paternal aunt.

questions.q: Five years ago, Sara was twice as old as Ali. Ali is 15 years old now. How old will Sara be three years from now?
questions.x: Five years ago Ali was 10, so Sara was 20; she is 25 now and will be 28 in three years.

questions.q: Statement: A teacher found one student sleeping during a lecture. Courses of action: I. All lectures should be shortened to ten minutes. II. The student should be expelled from the college. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: One sleepy student does not justify changing every lecture, and expulsion is far too harsh for this. Neither action follows.

questions.q: Statement: A college's pass rate in physics fell after its only physics teacher left in the middle of the year. Courses of action: I. The college should appoint a new physics teacher quickly. II. Extra classes should be arranged for students who missed lessons. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: Appointing a teacher fixes the cause for the future, and extra classes repair the lessons already lost. Both follow from the information.

questions.q: Statement I: A new mobile phone model went on sale in Karachi. Statement II: The wheat harvest in Punjab was good this year. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Both statements are effects of independent causes
questions.x: A phone launch and a good harvest have no link with each other and no shared cause. Each has its own separate reason.

questions.q: Statement I: A village started classes to teach adults to read. Statement II: More villagers began reading the health leaflets given out at the local clinic. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Both statements are effects of independent causes
Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
questions.x: Learning to read made it possible for adults to use the leaflets. The classes came first and caused the change.
